content.text: The text reviews gastric ulcer, gastric cancer, gastric hemorrhage, and gastric dilatation. Gastric ulcer is most common between ages 20–60, especially in women aged 20–30 and men aged 30–40; symptoms include meal-related epigastric pain, vomiting, dyspepsia, hemorrhage, and possible perforation. Most ulcers heal, but recurrence, stenosis, hemorrhage, and peritonitis are serious complications. Treatment emphasizes rest, bland milk-based nutrition, rectal feeding when necessary, symptom control, and cautious surgery for perforation or obstruction. Gastric cancer chiefly affects older adults, especially ages 40–70, commonly involves the pylorus, and causes progressive anorexia, vomiting, pain, tumor, cachexia, anemia, and metastases. It is generally fatal, though rare early resection may help. Gastric hemorrhage most often arises from ulcer or cancer. Gastric dilatation results from pyloric obstruction, excessive or fermenting contents, or muscular weakness, producing delayed emptying, large-volume vomiting, splash sounds, and wasting.
